name: Factory
tagline: Droids for coding, migration, testing, and development workflows

tiers.notes: Exact numeric quotas are not publicly stated.

tiers.name: Enterprise

pricing.billingTerms: monthly self-serve plans; no public annual plan; Business and Enterprise are custom
pricing.hiddenCosts: Extra Usage is prepaid with a $10 minimum; Missions require Extra Usage, so the subscription price is not a complete ceiling. Purchased Extra Usage does not expire.

verdictSummary: Do not mistake the interface for the product. Factory's durable value is model, context, integration, which a solo one-shot build cannot reproduce responsibly. The prompt therefore builds only the closest honest personal consolation tool.
coreLoopDIY: Build a repository-local software development agents assistant that indexes one codebase, calls one model, proposes diffs, runs tests, and records every change.
diyTimeEstimate: not a true replacement; consolation build in one to two days
replacementScope: consolation build only; the paid product's moat remains
requirements: Explicit README warning that this is a consolation build, not a production replacement
whyPeopleStillPay: Factory: Developers pay for reliable context assembly, fast models, editor integration, evaluations, and safe handling of complex repositories.
ongoingBurden: Maintain model adapters, token budgets, indexing, sandboxing, diff application, test runners, and editor integrations.

priorArt.name: Continue
priorArt.desc: Open-source coding assistant for editors and terminals.

priorArt.name: Aider
priorArt.desc: Open-source terminal coding agent with repository-aware edits.

alternatives.name: Aider
alternatives.desc: It edits the repo from a terminal and commits its own mess.

facts.install: Python installer (pip install aider-install, then aider-install) or pipx
facts.engines: LiteLLM-backed providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter, Azure, Bedrock, Groq and OpenAI-compatible endpoints, plus Ollama and other local models
facts.dataFormat: Edits and Git commits stay in the local repository; chat/input history is stored in local dotfiles, while selected code and prompts are sent to the configured model backend
facts.gapVsPaid: It is one supervised terminal agent, not Factory's centrally managed fleet of reusable Droids and organization workflows.
facts.setupBlocker: A terminal, a Git repository, and either a provider API key or a working local model server

alternatives.name: Cline
alternatives.desc: A code agent in your editor; the model bill is still yours.

facts.install: Install from the VS Code or JetBrains marketplace, or install the Cline CLI
facts.engines: Cline account models or bring-your-own-key providers including Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Azure, Bedrock, Vertex and OpenRouter, plus local Ollama and LM Studio models
facts.dataFormat: Repository edits stay in the local workspace; extension/session settings are local, while selected workspace context and prompts go to the chosen model provider
facts.gapVsPaid: It is a per-editor agent without Factory's shared Droid catalog, managed queues and organization-level orchestration.
facts.setupBlocker: Sign in to Cline or configure a provider API key or local model

alternatives.name: Goose
alternatives.desc: A desktop agent that edits and runs code without pretending the model is free.

facts.install: Download the desktop app or use Homebrew/packages; the CLI also has an install script
facts.engines: More than 15 providers including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Ollama, OpenRouter, Azure, Bedrock and ACP or subscription-backed agents; tools connect through MCP
facts.dataFormat: Sessions live in a local SQLite database under the user's Goose data directory and can be exported as JSON or Markdown; configuration is local and prompts go to the selected provider
facts.gapVsPaid: It handles local tasks well but does not provide Factory's managed fleet for migrations, testing and repeatable team workflows.
facts.setupBlocker: Configure a model provider key, supported subscription, or local model before useful work begins

alternatives.name: Kilo Code
alternatives.desc: Reusable coding agents across editors and terminal, without Factory's managed fleet.

alternatives.name: OpenCode
alternatives.desc: A fast local coding agent with no loyalty to any model vendor.

facts.install: Install with the shell script, Homebrew, npm or Bun; a desktop app is also available
facts.engines: A broad provider catalog covering hosted, OpenAI-compatible and local model endpoints, including optional OpenCode Zen or Go services
facts.dataFormat: Project files remain local; configuration, sessions and snapshot metadata are local, and a session is uploaded only when the user explicitly shares it, while prompts go to the chosen provider
facts.gapVsPaid: It is a single local agent rather than a centrally managed Droid fleet with reusable organization workflows and governance.
facts.setupBlocker: Configure a provider credential or local model unless using a separately billed OpenCode model service

alternatives.name: OpenHands
alternatives.desc: A self-hosted coding-agent control room for delegated repository work; Docker is the admission fee.

facts.install: Install Agent Canvas with npm (Node 22.12+ and uv) or run the official Docker image
facts.engines: OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini and other ACP-compatible agents, using model profiles and API credentials configured for each backend
facts.dataFormat: Projects are mounted or accessed locally and state and credentials live under the user's .openhands directory; OpenHands Cloud stores managed conversations in its service
facts.gapVsPaid: It can coordinate agents, but the user operates the control plane and gets less polished enterprise Droid governance and support.
facts.setupBlocker: Node plus uv or Docker, agent/model credentials, and a deliberate choice between full-access local execution and a sandboxed backend

rejectedAlternatives.name: Continue
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Acquired by Cursor; the repo is read-only and 2.0.0 is the last release.

notes: Credibility row: Factory survives for a structural reason, not because its interface is difficult to copy.
prompt:
Build the closest honest consolation tool inspired by Factory; do not claim to replace its structural moat.
Use exactly this stack: Python 3.12 + Typer + SQLite.
Primary job: Build a repository-local software development agents assistant that indexes one codebase, calls one model, proposes diffs, runs tests, and records every change.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: frontier coding model quality; large-context infrastructure; IDE-wide polish and latency.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
